Morocco is one of those places that feels impossibly far from home and then, three hours after landing, feels like somewhere you've always wanted to be. For a first-time American traveler, it's an easy introduction to North Africa and the Arab world: it's set up for tourism, the distances are manageable, and you can pack sweeping desert, medieval cities, and Atlantic beaches into a single trip. This guide covers the things first-timers actually worry about, so you can plan with confidence rather than guesswork.

Do Americans need a visa for Morocco?

No. U.S. citizens can enter Morocco visa-free for tourism and stay up to 90 days. You'll get a stamp on arrival; there's no fee and no online application to fill out beforehand. That said, entry rules are the one thing worth double-checking close to your trip, since governments change them without much notice. Make sure your passport is valid for at least six months beyond your entry date and has a blank page for the stamp. We cover the details in our Morocco visa guide for Americans.

Is Morocco safe?

For the vast majority of visitors, yes. Violent crime against tourists is rare, and Morocco is generally considered one of the safer countries in the region — millions of travelers, including solo women, visit every year without incident. What you'll actually deal with is petty stuff: pickpocketing in crowds, aggressive touts, and medina scams like a stranger insisting a street is "closed" so they can lead you somewhere. None of it is dangerous, but it's worth knowing about so it doesn't rattle you. Our honest safety guide walks through it, and the common scams are easy to sidestep once you know the playbook.

Money: the dirham is a closed currency

The Moroccan dirham is a closed currency, so you cannot buy it before you fly — no US bank sells it. You withdraw dirham from an ATM once you land (there are machines in the Casablanca and Marrakech arrival halls) or change dollars at a licensed bureau. Morocco runs heavily on cash: souks, taxis and small cafes are cash-only, while hotels and nicer restaurants take cards.

When should you visit?

Spring (March to May) and fall (September to November) are the sweet spots: warm days, cool nights, and comfortable conditions for both the cities and the desert. Summer gets brutally hot inland — Marrakech, Fez, and the Sahara can push past 100°F — though the coast at Essaouira stays mild. Winter is cool and pleasant in the cities, cold at night in the desert, and snowy in the Atlas Mountains. If your dates overlap Ramadan, the rhythm of daily life changes; it's a fascinating time to visit but worth understanding first. See our month-by-month guide.

Where to go on a first trip

A first trip usually covers four places in ten days or fewer: Marrakech as the entry point, Fez for the medieval medina, Chefchaouen in the Rif mountains, and one night in the Sahara. Each is completely different from the last, and the distances between them shape the itinerary more than the sights do. The classic loop, in order:

Marrakech

The sensory heart of Morocco and the usual starting point, with the famous Jemaa el-Fnaa square, endless souks, and gorgeous gardens. See our Marrakech guide.

Fez

Home to the world's largest car-free medieval city — a genuine maze where a local guide for the first day pays for itself.

Chefchaouen

The blue-washed mountain town, small, relaxed, and endlessly photogenic.

The Sahara

A night in a desert camp among the dunes of Erg Chebbi is the bucket-list experience — camel ride at sunset, dinner under the stars, sunrise over the sand.

Essaouira and the Atlas Mountains

A windswept Atlantic beach town and the Berber villages of the High Atlas round out the trip if you have time.

Getting around

Morocco is easier to navigate than you'd expect. Comfortable ONCF trains connect Casablanca, Rabat, Fez, and Marrakech, with a high-speed line up north. For places off the rail network — Chefchaouen, Essaouira, and the desert gateways — CTM and Supratours coaches are the reliable options. In cities, small metered "petit taxis" handle short hops (insist on the meter or agree the fare first). The Sahara is almost always done as a multi-day tour with a driver. More in our transport guide.

Language: will you get by?

Yes. Arabic and Tamazight (Berber) are the official languages, and French is widely spoken in business, government, and tourism — a legacy you'll notice on signs and menus. In the places tourists spend time, English is common: hotel and riad staff, guides, and popular restaurants will usually handle English fine. Away from the tourist track, a few words of French go further than English, and any attempt at Arabic — a simple "salam" (hello) or "shukran" (thank you) — is warmly received. You don't need to speak the language to travel here comfortably, but a handful of phrases makes every interaction friendlier.

What a first trip actually feels like

Set your expectations for contrast, because that's the Morocco experience. One hour you're haggling for a lantern in a chaotic souk with a dozen smells competing for your attention; the next you're sipping tea in silent riad courtyard. The cities are intense and can be tiring — the constant sensory input and the occasional tout wear on you — so build in downtime and don't try to cram every day full. The desert and mountains, by contrast, are serene. A well-paced first trip alternates the two, and most people leave already planning a return.

Practical first-timer tips

A few things that smooth out a first trip: dress modestly, especially outside tourist zones — covering shoulders and knees is respectful and also helps with sun and heat. Get an eSIM so you land connected, which is handy when you need maps or a ride the moment you arrive and don't have dirham yet. Accept the mint tea when it's offered; it's hospitality, not a sales trap. And decide early whether you want a guided tour or independent travel — both work well here, and it shapes how you book everything else. The connections between these decisions — base, route, desert, money — are worked out together in the complete Morocco trip guide.

Morocco first-timer FAQ

How many days do you need for a first trip to Morocco?

Seven days covers a solid taste (two cities plus a desert night); ten days is the comfortable classic loop; two weeks lets you add the coast and mountains without rushing.

Can you drink alcohol in Morocco?

Yes — it's legal for tourists and served in many hotels, licensed restaurants, and bars, though it's not consumed openly in public. It's simply less visible than at home.

Do people speak English in Morocco?

Arabic and Tamazight are official, and French is widely used. English is common in tourist areas — hotels, guides, and popular restaurants — though a few French or Arabic phrases go a long way elsewhere.

Is Morocco good for a first international trip?

It's a great step beyond Europe: exotic and different, but well set up for tourists, with short distances and plenty of infrastructure. A little preparation goes a long way.

Marrakech is where most first trips to Morocco begin, and for good reason — it's the country's sensory heart, a swirl of souks, palaces, gardens, and one of the most famous squares on earth. It can also be gloriously overwhelming on day one. This guide sets you up to enjoy Marrakech rather than just survive it.

Getting to Marrakech

You can fly straight into Marrakech Menara (RAK), which is what most first-timers doing the classic loop do — it saves the transfer from Casablanca. If you land at Casablanca instead, a comfortable ONCF train reaches Marrakech in about three hours. The airport is only about fifteen minutes from the medina; arrange a pickup through your riad for the smoothest arrival, since finding a specific riad in the medina maze with luggage is the one genuinely tricky first-day moment. Our flights guide covers routing from the U.S.

The top things to see

Marrakech's essential sights sit close together: Jemaa el-Fnaa and the souks immediately north of it, the Koutoubia minaret on the square's western edge, and the Bahia Palace and Saadian Tombs to the south. The Majorelle Garden is the one that needs a taxi. Two full days covers all of it without rushing, which leaves room for the aimless wandering that makes the city. The essentials:

Jemaa el-Fnaa

The legendary main square — sleepy by day, electric at dusk when food stalls, musicians, and storytellers take over. Watch it fill up from a rooftop cafe with a mint tea, then dive in.

The souks

The labyrinth of markets north of the square, selling everything from lanterns and leather to spices and rugs. Getting lost here is the point; haggling is expected (our haggling guide helps).

Palaces and gardens

The ornate Bahia Palace, the serene Saadian Tombs, the historic Ben Youssef Madrasa with its dazzling tilework, and the cobalt-blue Majorelle Garden (and the adjacent YSL museum) for a calm, green break. The Koutoubia minaret anchors the skyline — you can admire it from outside, though the mosque itself isn't open to non-Muslims.

For a fuller run-down, see our dedicated things to do in Marrakech.

Where to stay

Your base shapes the whole experience. The classic choice is a riad in the medina — steps from the action, atmospheric, and a quiet courtyard retreat from the bustle. If you'd rather have modern hotels, restaurants, and easier logistics, Gueliz (the Ville Nouvelle) is the modern district; Hivernage is upscale and quieter; and the Palmeraie offers resort-style stays outside the center. Most first-timers pick a medina riad for the atmosphere. Our where to stay in Marrakech guide breaks down the areas.

Day trips from Marrakech

Marrakech is the launchpad for some of Morocco's best excursions. The Ourika Valley and Atlas foothills are an easy 1–1.5 hours out for Berber villages and waterfalls; the Agafay stone desert offers a close sunset-camp experience without the long desert drive; Essaouira on the coast makes a good full-day escape; and the Sahara at Merzouga is the big one — a multi-day guided trip (see our Sahara tours from Marrakech guide).

Handling the hustle

Marrakech is friendly but also the most touristed city in Morocco, which means touts, faux guides, and the occasional scam. None of it is dangerous — a firm, polite "la shukran" (no thank you) and walking on handles most of it. Ignore anyone insisting a street or sight is "closed," agree taxi fares before getting in, and settle a price before any photo with a performer. Our safety guide preps you fully. Go in expecting a bit of theater and it becomes part of the fun rather than a stressor.

Getting around Marrakech

The medina is car-free and best explored on foot — expect to walk a lot, and wear comfortable shoes for the uneven lanes. For longer hops (to Gueliz, the Majorelle Garden, or the train station), small metered petit taxis are cheap; insist on the meter or agree the fare first, as some drivers will claim it's broken. Horse-drawn carriages (calèches) are a touristy but pleasant way to loop the ramparts. Ride-hail apps operate in the city too. One tip: note a nearby landmark or gate for your riad, because GPS struggles in the dense medina and you'll navigate the last stretch on foot by feel.

Eating in Marrakech

Marrakech is a fantastic place to eat, from street food to refined rooftop dining. Start with the Jemaa el-Fnaa food stalls for atmosphere (choose busy ones), graduate to rooftop riad restaurants for tagine with a view, and seek out the modern Moroccan spots in Gueliz for a calmer sit-down meal. Don't miss street classics like fresh orange juice from the square, msemen (flaky pancakes) at breakfast, and a pastry with mint tea in the afternoon. A cooking class or food tour is a great way to go deeper — our guide to Moroccan dishes tells you what to order.

Best time to visit Marrakech

Marrakech is at its best in spring (March–May) and fall (September–November), when days are warm and evenings pleasant. Summer is intensely hot — often over 100°F — which makes midday sightseeing tough, though early mornings, late evenings, and shady riad courtyards with plunge pools help. Winter days are mild and sunny but nights get cold, so pack layers. The city runs year-round, but timing your visit for the shoulder seasons makes the walking, the souks, and the day trips far more comfortable; see our when-to-go guide for the full picture.

How long to stay

Two to three days is right for a first visit — enough for the sights, the souks, an evening or two at Jemaa el-Fnaa, and a day trip. It's also the natural starting point before heading to the desert and Fez, as laid out in our 10-day itinerary. Give the city a relaxed first day to acclimate, and let the medina reveal itself slowly. How Marrakech fits the wider route is covered in the complete Morocco trip guide.

Marrakech FAQ

How many days do you need in Marrakech?

Two to three days covers the main sights, the souks, Jemaa el-Fnaa, and a day trip — and it's the ideal launch point for the desert and Fez.

Where should first-timers stay in Marrakech?

Most choose a riad in the medina for the atmosphere and central location. Gueliz suits those who prefer modern hotels and easier logistics.

Is Marrakech safe for tourists?

Yes, with normal precautions. The main issues are touts and scams, not danger — a polite refusal and settling prices in advance handle most of it.

What's the best day trip from Marrakech?

The Atlas Mountains (Ourika Valley) for an easy day out, or a multi-day Sahara tour to Merzouga for the bucket-list desert night.

Marrakech packs an enormous amount into a compact old city, and a first-timer can easily fill two or three days without repeating a thing. Here are the best things to do, from the unmissable icons to the smaller pleasures that make the city special.

Experience Jemaa el-Fnaa at dusk

The city's beating heart and the thing to do first. By day it's a wide, sun-baked square with juice stalls and snake charmers; at sunset it transforms into a carnival of food stalls, musicians, and storytellers. The move is to watch it fill up from a rooftop terrace cafe with a mint tea, then descend into the crowd. Eat at a busy food stall, keep an eye on your belongings, and soak up an atmosphere that's been going for centuries.

Get lost in the souks

The maze of covered markets stretching north from the square is a highlight in itself. Each area specializes — leather, lanterns, spices, carpets, metalwork — and haggling is expected and part of the fun (our haggling guide gives you the playbook). Don't over-plan; wandering and getting pleasantly lost is exactly the right way to experience them.

Tour the palaces and historic sites

Marrakech's architecture is stunning up close. The Bahia Palace is a 19th-century showpiece of painted ceilings and courtyards. The Saadian Tombs hide dazzling tilework behind a narrow passage. The Ben Youssef Madrasa, a former Quranic school, is one of the most beautiful buildings in the country. And the Koutoubia minaret — the city's tallest landmark — anchors the skyline, best admired from outside as the mosque is closed to non-Muslims.

Find calm in the gardens

When the medina's intensity gets to you, the gardens are the antidote. The Majorelle Garden, painted its famous cobalt blue, is a cool botanical oasis, with the Yves Saint Laurent museum next door. The Menara Gardens and Le Jardin Secret offer more green respite. These make perfect mid-afternoon breaks from the heat and the crowds.

Soak in a hammam

A traditional hammam (steam bath and scrub) is a quintessential North African experience and a wonderful way to unwind after days of walking. Options range from local public hammams to luxurious spa versions in riads and hotels — first-timers often prefer the gentler spa route. It's relaxing, cultural, and leaves you feeling brand new. First-timers should know the basic ritual: you'll steam to soften the skin, get scrubbed with black soap and a coarse glove (kessa) that removes astonishing amounts of dead skin, rinse, and often finish with an argan-oil massage. In a public hammam you bring your own toiletries and it's gender-separated; in a spa version everything is provided and it's more pampering than authentic. Either way, it's an experience worth having at least once.

Take a cooking class or food tour

Moroccan cuisine is a trip highlight, and a hands-on cooking class — often starting with a souk shopping trip — teaches you to make tagine and other staples while demystifying the ingredients. Food tours of the medina are another great way to eat well and understand what you're tasting. Our guide to Moroccan dishes tells you what to look for.

Escape on a day trip

If you have an extra day, Marrakech is the springboard for great excursions — the Atlas foothills and Ourika Valley for mountain scenery, the Agafay desert for a close sunset-camp experience, or Essaouira on the coast. The big one, of course, is a multi-day trip to the Sahara; see our Sahara tours guide.

Shop for Moroccan crafts

Marrakech is one of the best places in the country to shop, and the crafts are genuinely special: hand-knotted rugs, leather bags and poufs, brass and silver lanterns, ceramics, babouche slippers, and argan-oil products. Prices are almost always negotiable, so haggling is expected — start well below the asking price and settle somewhere in the middle, always with good humor. If big-ticket items like rugs feel intimidating, the fixed-price artisan cooperatives (Ensemble Artisanal) are a low-pressure way to gauge fair prices before you dive into the souks. Our haggling guide walks through the etiquette.

Watch a sunset from the ramparts or a rooftop

Marrakech glows at golden hour. The city's red-earth walls and the palm groves take on a warm light, and a rooftop terrace above the medina — mint tea in hand, the call to prayer echoing across the rooftops, the Atlas Mountains sometimes visible in the distance — is one of those simple travel moments that stays with you. Many riads and cafes have rooftop terraces open to the public; it's the perfect way to bookend a busy day of sightseeing before heading down to Jemaa el-Fnaa for the evening.

Day and evening rhythm

A smart way to structure a Marrakech day is to work with the heat and the city's rhythm rather than against it. Sightsee the palaces, madrasas, and gardens in the cooler morning hours, retreat to your riad or a shady cafe for lunch and a rest during the hottest part of the afternoon, then re-emerge in the late afternoon for the souks and a rooftop sunset before Jemaa el-Fnaa comes alive at dusk. This gentle pacing keeps you from burning out — the city is intense, and trying to power through midday heat is how first-timers end up exhausted by day two. Build in the downtime and you'll enjoy it far more.

Enjoy the rooftops

Some of Marrakech's best moments are simply sitting on a rooftop terrace above the medina — a coffee in the morning, a sunset drink, dinner overlooking the square. Many riads and cafes have them, and they offer a calm bird's-eye view of a city that's anything but calm at street level. Plan your visit around our complete Marrakech guide. Which of these earn a ticket and which reward a wander is worked through in the complete Morocco trip guide.

Things to do in Marrakech FAQ

What is Marrakech best known for?

The Jemaa el-Fnaa square, its sprawling souks, ornate palaces and gardens, and as the launch point for Atlas and Sahara excursions.

What should you not miss in Marrakech?

Jemaa el-Fnaa at dusk, the souks, the Bahia Palace and Ben Youssef Madrasa, the Majorelle Garden, and a traditional hammam.

Is two days enough for Marrakech?

Two days covers the essentials; three lets you add a hammam, a cooking class, or a day trip at a relaxed pace.

What's a good rainy-day or heat-break activity?

A hammam, a cooking class, or the gardens and museums — all pleasant escapes from midday heat or the occasional wet day.

If Marrakech is Morocco's showman, Fez is its scholar — older, deeper, and more traditional. Home to the world's largest car-free urban area, Fez is a living medieval city that many travelers end up loving even more than Marrakech. It's also the most bewildering to navigate, so a little preparation goes a long way.

Getting to Fez

Fez is well connected: comfortable ONCF trains run from Casablanca, Rabat, and Marrakech, or you can fly into Fez–Saïss (FEZ), useful if you're running the classic loop in reverse. Fez pairs naturally with Chefchaouen, about four hours north by bus. On a typical first-timer loop, many travelers arrive in Fez after the desert and leave from here or continue north. Our flights guide covers open-jaw routing.

The medina: embrace the maze

Fès el-Bali, the old medina, is the main event — a warren of thousands of narrow lanes with no cars, where donkeys still haul goods and it's genuinely easy to lose all sense of direction. This is not a flaw; it's the experience. That said, hiring a licensed local guide for your first morning is money exceptionally well spent: they orient you, get you past the faux-guide hustle, and open doors you'd walk right past. After that you can explore on your own with an offline map and a relaxed attitude toward getting lost.

What to see in Fez

The Chouara Tannery

Fez's iconic image — centuries-old stone dye pits worked by hand, best viewed from the terraces of the surrounding leather shops (you'll be handed a sprig of mint for the smell). Expect a sales pitch upstairs; enjoy the view, buy if you like, no pressure to.

The madrasas

The Bou Inania and Al-Attarine madrasas are jewels of Marinid craftsmanship — intricate zellij tile, carved cedar, and stucco. Small but breathtaking.

Al-Qarawiyyin

Founded in 859, considered one of the oldest continuously operating universities in the world. Non-Muslims can't enter the mosque but can glimpse the courtyard.

Bab Bou Jeloud

The grand tiled Blue Gate that marks the western entrance to the medina — a classic first stop and orientation point.

Where to stay

Stay in a riad inside Fès el-Bali for the full immersion — restored courtyard houses tucked into the medina, with staff who'll help you navigate. If you prefer modern comfort and easier access, the Ville Nouvelle (Fès el-Jdid and beyond) has conventional hotels. Most first-timers choose the medina riad for atmosphere.

Day trips from Fez

Two stand out. Meknes and the Roman ruins of Volubilis make a rewarding full day — an imperial city plus remarkably intact mosaics, an easy trip from Fez. And Chefchaouen, the blue city, is a few hours north; while it's often an overnight rather than a day trip, some visit from Fez. See our Chefchaouen guide.

Eating in Fez

Fez is considered the culinary capital of Morocco, and its signature dish is pastilla (bastilla) — a remarkable sweet-and-savory pie of poultry, almonds, and cinnamon wrapped in flaky pastry and dusted with sugar. Beyond that, the city's riads and restaurants serve some of the country's finest traditional cooking: slow-cooked tagines, harira soup, and elaborate multi-course meals in restored palaces. Because the medina is a maze, having your riad recommend and even reserve a dinner spot saves you wandering hungry. Street food and hole-in-the-wall spots near Bab Bou Jeloud are cheap and good for lunch. See our guide to Moroccan dishes.

Etiquette in a traditional city

Fez is more conservative and less touristy than Marrakech, so a little cultural awareness goes further here. Dress modestly — cover shoulders and knees — especially away from the main tourist lanes. Ask before photographing people, particularly in the residential heart of the medina where daily life goes on around you. Non-Muslims can't enter the mosques, so admire them from doorways and courtyards. And accept that the medina is a living, working city, not a museum — donkeys have right of way, workshops spill into the lanes, and that authenticity is exactly what makes Fez special. Our etiquette guide covers the basics.

Getting around Fez

Inside Fès el-Bali there is no getting around except on foot — no cars, and the lanes are too narrow and steep for anything but walking (and the occasional donkey). Wear sturdy, comfortable shoes; the medina is hilly and the ground uneven. For travel between the medina and the Ville Nouvelle or the train station, petit taxis are cheap and plentiful — agree the fare or ask for the meter. Because addresses are meaningless in the maze, note the nearest gate (bab) to your riad and let staff guide you in on arrival. An offline map helps, but don't rely on GPS to be precise between the tall medina walls.

How long to stay

Two nights (one full day and a bit) is the sweet spot for a first visit — enough to do a guided morning, explore the tanneries and madrasas, and wander at leisure. Fez is quieter and more conservative than Marrakech, and less relentlessly touristy, which many find a welcome contrast. Fit it into your route with our 10-day itinerary. A common first-timer pattern is to arrive in Fez from the desert, spend two nights, then continue north to Chefchaouen or fly out — Fez makes a natural, satisfying end to the classic loop, sending you home with the memory of Morocco at its most timeless. Fez's place in a first-timer loop is set out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

Fez FAQ

Do you need a guide in Fez?

Not required, but highly recommended for your first morning — the medina is a genuine labyrinth, and a good guide orients you and fends off faux guides. After that you can explore solo.

How many days do you need in Fez?

Two nights is ideal — a guided morning plus free time for the tanneries, madrasas, and medina wandering.

Is Fez better than Marrakech?

Different, not better. Fez is older, more traditional, and less touristy; Marrakech is livelier and more set up for visitors. Many first-timers do both and love the contrast.

Can you visit the tanneries in Fez?

Yes — view the Chouara tannery from the terraces of surrounding leather shops. Expect a sales pitch, but there's no obligation to buy.

Tucked into the Rif Mountains of northern Morocco, Chefchaouen — the famous "Blue City" — is unlike anywhere else in the country. Its medina is washed in every shade of blue, from powder to cobalt, spilling down the hillside in a photographer's dream. Small, relaxed, and refreshingly low-hassle, it's the gentle counterpoint to the intensity of Marrakech and Fez.

How to get to Chefchaouen

Chefchaouen has no airport or train station, so you'll arrive by road. The reliable options are a CTM or Supratours bus, or a grand taxi, from Fez (about four hours) or Tangier (about two hours). It's most often visited as part of a northern leg — either after Fez heading north, or on the way to or from Tangier. Because it's a bit off the main loop, factor the travel time in; plenty of first-timers skip it on a short trip and prioritize it on a longer one. Our detailed transport guide covers the routes.

What to see and do

Wander the blue medina

The main activity is simply strolling the blue-washed lanes, and it's wonderful. Every corner, staircase, and doorway is a different shade, often framed with potted plants and hanging rugs. Mornings are quietest and best for photos before the day-trippers arrive.

Plaza Uta el-Hammam and the Kasbah

The lively central square, ringed with cafes, anchored by a red-walled kasbah with a small museum and garden you can climb for views.

The Spanish Mosque viewpoint

A short uphill walk from the medina leads to this hilltop mosque, the spot for sunset views over the whole blue town — don't miss it.

Ras el-Maa waterfall

At the medina's edge, this little cascade is where locals gather and do laundry; a pleasant, shaded place to pause.

Eating in Chefchaouen

The food scene is relaxed and affordable, with a northern, mountain character. Goat cheese is a local specialty — the region is known for it — and you'll find it in salads and on breakfast spreads. The main square, Plaza Uta el-Hammam, is ringed with cafes perfect for a leisurely tagine while people-watching, and rooftop terraces offer meals with a view over the blue rooftops. Prices are lower than in Marrakech or Fez, and the pace is unhurried. As a mountain town it also has a mellow cafe culture; lingering over mint tea and watching the light change on the blue walls is very much the local rhythm.

Where to stay

Small guesthouses and riads inside the blue medina are the charming choice — many with rooftop terraces overlooking the town. Staying in the medina lets you enjoy the lanes in the quiet early morning and evening after the day crowds thin. Options are simpler and more affordable than in the big cities, in keeping with the town's laid-back feel.

A day hike in the Rif

If you have an extra day and like the outdoors, the surrounding Rif Mountains offer good hiking. The most popular is the trek to the Akchour waterfalls and the "God's Bridge" rock arch — a rewarding day out in nature, easily arranged from town. It's a nice way to see a different side of the region beyond the blue streets.

Is Chefchaouen touristy?

Chefchaouen has become famous largely thanks to social media, and midday can bring day-trippers and photographers to the most Instagrammed corners. But it remains far more laid-back than the big cities, with noticeably less hustle — vendors are gentler, and the overall vibe is calm. The trick is timing: the medina is magical and near-empty in the early morning and evening, so staying overnight (rather than day-tripping) lets you enjoy the blue lanes at their most peaceful, bookended around the busier middle of the day. That contrast is exactly why an overnight beats a rushed visit.

How long to stay

One night (a full afternoon and the next morning) is enough for most to soak up Chefchaouen's charm — arrive in time for a sunset at the Spanish Mosque, wander the lanes at golden hour and again early the next day before crowds build. Add a second night if you want to hike the Rif or simply linger in the relaxed pace. It slots naturally into a northern extension of the classic loop. Many first-timers pair it with Fez, combining the two on the northern portion of their trip before flying home from Fez or continuing to Tangier. However you fit it in, Chefchaouen offers something the rest of the itinerary doesn't — a slow, blue-tinted breather amid the mountains that many travelers end up remembering as their favorite stop.

Practical tips for your visit

A few things to know before you go. Wear comfortable shoes — the medina is steep and cobbled, climbing the hillside. Bring some cash, as the town is small and card acceptance is limited outside hotels. The best photo light is early morning, before day-trippers arrive and while the blue walls glow softly. Buy your onward bus ticket (especially back to Fez) a day ahead in busy season, since seats are limited. And take it slow — Chefchaouen isn't a checklist destination; its whole appeal is the relaxed, wander-and-linger pace. Bring a light jacket even in warmer months, since the mountain setting means evenings cool down noticeably. Half the pleasure is simply sitting with a mint tea and watching the blue town go about its day.

Chefchaouen FAQ

How do you get to Chefchaouen?

By road only — CTM or Supratours bus, or a grand taxi, from Fez (about 4 hours) or Tangier (about 2 hours). There's no airport or train.

Is Chefchaouen worth visiting?

If you have the time, yes — it's uniquely beautiful, relaxed, and low-hassle. On a short trip it's often skipped in favor of the desert and imperial cities.

How long do you need in Chefchaouen?

One night suffices for the blue medina and a sunset viewpoint; a second night lets you hike the surrounding Rif Mountains.

Why is Chefchaouen blue?

Theories vary — from keeping cool and repelling mosquitoes to spiritual symbolism introduced by past communities. Whatever the origin, the whole medina is now famously painted blue.

For many first-time visitors, a night in the Sahara is the single most memorable part of a Morocco trip — a camel ride over golden dunes at sunset, dinner around a fire, and a sky thick with stars. It's also the leg that takes the most planning, since the desert is a long way from the cities. Here's what you need to know.

Merzouga or Zagora?

Merzouga is the right answer for most first-timers: Erg Chebbi's tall dunes are the postcard Sahara, and reaching them means a 9–10 hour drive from Marrakech, so realistically a 3-day/2-night trip. Zagora is closer and fits a 2-day/1-night trip, but its dunes are smaller and stonier. The choice is really about how many days you can give the desert.

Merzouga (Erg Chebbi)

Home to Erg Chebbi, the tall, sweeping golden dunes that look like the postcard Sahara. It's farther from Marrakech — roughly a 9–10 hour drive, so realistically a 3-day/2-night trip — but the dunes are dramatically bigger and more beautiful. For most first-timers chasing the classic desert image, Merzouga is worth the extra time.

Zagora

Closer to Marrakech and doable as a shorter 2-day/1-night trip, but the dunes are smaller and less spectacular, and the landscape is more rocky desert than towering sand. Choose Zagora if you're truly short on time; choose Merzouga if you can spare the extra day. Our detailed comparison goes deeper.

How to get there

There's no airport or train to the dunes — the Sahara is reached overland, almost always as a guided multi-day tour with a driver, or self-driven if you're adventurous. Most first-timers take the tour, because it handles the long distances and turns the drive itself into part of the trip, with spectacular stops along the way: the film-famous kasbah of Aït Benhaddou, the dramatic Todra Gorge, and the Dades and Rose valleys. See our Sahara tours from Marrakech guide for how to book.

What a desert camp night is like

The heart of the experience. In the late afternoon you'll ride a camel (or 4x4) into the dunes to your camp as the light turns gold. Camps range from simple to genuinely luxurious, but the rhythm is similar: a traditional dinner, often music around a fire, and then the main event — lying back under a sky so full of stars it's disorienting. Nights can be cold, even in summer, so layers matter. In the morning, wake for sunrise over the dunes, one of the great sights of any trip.

What to pack for the desert

A few essentials make the trip far more comfortable: layers for hot days and genuinely cold nights, a scarf (invaluable against sun and blowing sand), sunglasses and sunscreen, closed shoes plus sandals, a headlamp or flashlight, and any cash you'll need since there are no ATMs out here. Bring a small bag for the camp and leave your main luggage in the vehicle. And download offline maps and music before you go — there's little to no signal in the deep desert.

The camel ride: what it's really like

The sunset camel trek into the dunes is the iconic Sahara moment, and it's worth setting expectations. You'll ride single-file in a small caravan, led by a guide on foot, for anywhere from twenty minutes to an hour to reach camp. It's slower and more lurching than you might picture — camels rock as they stand and sit, so hold on during those moments — but the pace lets you soak in the shifting light on the dunes. If riding isn't for you (it can be uncomfortable for some backs and knees), most camps can arrange a 4x4 transfer instead, so you don't miss the camp itself. Either way, wear long pants and bring that scarf for the sand.

Simple vs. luxury desert camps

Where you sleep shapes the whole night. Basic camps offer simple tents with shared bathroom facilities and mattresses on the floor — perfectly fine for one night and cheaper. Mid-range and luxury camps have private tents with real beds, rugs, and sometimes en-suite bathrooms, plus better dinners and more comfort, for a surprisingly modest step up in price. Since this is likely your one and only desert night, many first-timers happily pay a little more for the upgrade. When you book a tour from Marrakech, check exactly which camp tier is included, as it's the biggest variable in the experience.

Is the Sahara trip suitable for everyone?

For most people, yes — but a few honest notes. The long drive and the camel ride can be tiring for very young children, older travelers, or anyone with back or mobility issues, though 4x4 transfers to camp and private tours ease this considerably. The desert is remote, with limited medical facilities and no reliable phone signal, so bring any needed medications and let someone know your plans. That said, families with kids often find the camels, dunes, and camp a huge hit, and the trip is a highlight across all ages. If a multi-day journey feels like too much, the Agafay stone desert near Marrakech offers a taste of a desert camp without the long haul, though it lacks the true Saharan dunes.

When to go

Spring (March–May) and fall (September–November) are ideal — warm days, cool but bearable nights. Summer days are brutally hot, though the dunes at sunset and night are still magical; winter nights are very cold. See our when-to-go guide to time it well. However you do it, a Sahara night tends to be the memory that outlasts all the others.

One thing worth noticing across all of this: the dune field you pick decides the length of the drive, the drive decides how many nights the desert costs you, and those nights decide what is left for the cities. The desert isn't a side trip you slot in — it is the piece the rest of the itinerary bends around. That whole chain is worked out, leg by leg, in the complete Morocco trip guide.

Sahara desert FAQ

Is Merzouga or Zagora better?

Merzouga has the tall, classic Erg Chebbi dunes but needs a 3-day trip; Zagora is closer and doable in 2 days but with smaller dunes. Most first-timers prefer Merzouga if time allows.

How many days do you need for the Sahara?

Merzouga is realistically a 3-day/2-night trip from Marrakech; Zagora can be done in 2 days/1 night.

Is a Sahara desert tour worth it?

For most first-timers it's the trip's highlight — the camel ride, camp dinner, stargazing, and sunrise over the dunes are unforgettable.

Is it cold in the Sahara at night?

Yes, often surprisingly cold even after hot days, and very cold in winter. Pack warm layers for the camp regardless of season.

Ten days is the sweet spot for a first trip to Morocco: enough to see the headline places without sprinting, enough to spend a night in the Sahara without the whole trip becoming a road trip. This is the classic first-timer loop — Marrakech, the Atlas, the desert, Fez, and the blue city of Chefchaouen — arranged so each place feels distinct and the travel days make sense.

Days 1–3: Marrakech

Start in Marrakech, the sensory heart of Morocco. Give yourself a day to settle into a riad and ease into the medina without a plan — get pleasantly lost, then find your bearings. On your full days, hit the highlights: the Bahia Palace, the cobalt-blue Majorelle Garden, the Koutoubia minaret, and the endless souks. Save an evening for Jemaa el-Fnaa, the famous square that transforms at dusk into a swirl of food stalls and performers. Use one day for an Atlas Mountains day trip — the Ourika Valley or Imlil are an easy 1–1.5 hours out, with Berber villages and waterfalls. Full details in our Marrakech guide.

Days 4–5: The Sahara

Days 4 and 5 are the Sahara crossing, and it is a proper journey rather than a day trip — most first-timers do it as a guided multi-day tour with a driver, which handles the long distances and the overnight stops. The route runs south over the High Atlas, through the Dades Valley, and into the dunes at Merzouga.

Day 4: the road south

Cross the High Atlas by the dramatic Tizi n'Tichka pass, stopping at Aït Benhaddou — the UNESCO earthen kasbah you've seen in countless films — then continue through the Dades Valley for an overnight along the way.

Day 5: into the dunes

Through the Todra Gorge and on to Merzouga at the edge of Erg Chebbi, the tall golden dunes that are the postcard Sahara. Late afternoon, ride a camel into the dunes to a desert camp for dinner, stargazing, and a night under more stars than you've ever seen. Wake for sunrise over the sand. Our Sahara guide covers what to pack and expect.

Days 6–7: Fez

From the desert, transfer to Fez (a long but scenic drive). Fez is home to the world's largest car-free medieval city — Fès el-Bali — a genuine labyrinth where hiring a local guide for your first morning is money well spent. See the famous Chouara tanneries from a surrounding terrace, the intricate madrasas, and the ancient Qarawiyyin. Fez is more traditional and less touristy than Marrakech, and many travelers find it their favorite. Base yourself in a medina riad for the atmosphere.

Days 8–9: Chefchaouen

Head north to Chefchaouen, the blue-washed mountain town, by bus or private transfer (there's no train). It's small, relaxed, and endlessly photogenic — a gentle change of pace after the intensity of the big cities. Wander the blue lanes, climb to the Spanish Mosque viewpoint for sunset over the rooftops, and if you want a hike, the Akchour waterfalls in the surrounding Rif Mountains make a good day out. This is the trip's exhale.

Day 10: Home

Make your way back toward Casablanca or Fez for your departure. If you built your flights as an open-jaw (into Marrakech, out of Casablanca or Fez), you avoid backtracking entirely — worth arranging when you book, as our flights guide explains.

Ways to customize this route

The 10-day loop is a template, not a rulebook, and a few swaps tailor it to your taste. If you'd rather have coast than blue city, drop Chefchaouen and add Essaouira as an overnight or a long day trip from Marrakech — a windswept, laid-back Atlantic town that's an easy change of pace. If you love mountains, trade a desert night for an extra day trekking or staying in the Atlas around Imlil. If cities tire you quickly, shorten Fez to one full day and add a slower stretch in Chefchaouen or the mountains. And if you're traveling with kids, build in more downtime — riad pools are a lifesaver in the afternoon heat, and the camel ride and desert camp are usually a hit. The bones of the route (Marrakech, desert, Fez) stay; the edges flex to you.

What each day actually feels like

Set expectations for the rhythm. The Marrakech days are intense and sensory — busy, hot, occasionally overwhelming in the best way — so you'll want your riad as a retreat. The desert days involve real driving, broken up by spectacular stops; the payoff of the dune night is worth every hour in the car. Fez is a slower burn: less flashy than Marrakech, deeper the more you look. Chefchaouen is the exhale — small, gentle, and photogenic. Understanding this arc helps you pace yourself: front-load energy for the cities and the desert, and let the northern leg be your wind-down.

Packing and pacing notes

A few practical things for this specific route. Pack layers — the desert swings from hot afternoons to genuinely cold nights, and the Atlas can be cool. Bring a scarf (useful for sun, dust, and modesty at religious sites), comfortable walking shoes for endless medina cobbles, and a small daypack. Keep some cash on you at all times, since much of this route is cash-only once you leave the hotels. And resist the urge to add a sixth destination; the strength of this itinerary is that it breathes. For the money side, our cost guide breaks down what the whole thing runs.

Why the order works

There's logic to the sequence beyond just geography. Starting in Marrakech eases you in through the most tourist-ready city, where riads, guides, and English are easiest. Doing the desert mid-trip means you've acclimated before the long drives, and you return to civilization in Fez rather than backtracking. Ending in Chefchaouen's calm sends you home relaxed rather than frazzled from a big-city finale. And the whole thing traces a rough line south then north, so an open-jaw flight (into Marrakech, out near Fez or Casablanca) means you never repeat a leg. Reverse it if your flights demand — the route works both directions — but this order gives the smoothest emotional and logistical arc for a first trip.

Tips for this route

Before the specifics, three things that quietly make or break the 10 days: get an eSIM so you land connected and can navigate from minute one; carry a stash of small dirham notes for the constant small payments this route involves; and book the desert tour and your riads well ahead, since the best small riads sell out in peak season and a good desert operator is worth securing early. With those handled, the rest of the trip runs on rails.

A few things that make the 10 days flow: consider a mix of guided and independent — a driver for the desert leg, independent time in the cities. Book riads early, especially in peak spring and fall. Pack layers: the desert is hot by day and cold at night, and the Atlas can be cool. And don't over-schedule the cities; the medinas reward wandering more than checklist-chasing. If you have only a week, our 7-day itinerary trims this down; with two weeks, the 14-day version adds the coast. The reasoning behind this order, and what breaks when you change it, is in the complete Morocco trip guide.

10-day Morocco itinerary FAQ

Is 10 days enough for Morocco?

Yes — 10 days is the ideal first-timer length. It covers Marrakech, the Atlas, a Sahara night, Fez, and Chefchaouen at a comfortable pace.

Should I book a tour or do this independently?

Most first-timers do a hybrid: a guided multi-day tour for the desert leg (it handles the long drives) and independent time in the cities.

Which direction should I travel the loop?

Either works. Starting in Marrakech and ending near Fez or Casablanca lets you fly open-jaw and avoid backtracking.

How much does a 10-day Morocco trip cost?

A mid-range trip runs roughly $1,000–1,600 per person on the ground plus flights. See our full cost breakdown for budget and luxury ranges.

A week isn't a lot of time for a country as varied as Morocco, but it's enough to come home with the essential experience: the buzz of Marrakech, a night under the stars in the Sahara, and the medieval maze of Fez. This 7-day itinerary is built for first-timers who want the highlights without feeling like they spent the whole trip in transit.

The strategy: don't try to do everything

The single biggest mistake on a 7-day Morocco trip is cramming in too much and spending your week in a car. This route deliberately skips Chefchaouen and the coast (save those for a longer trip) and focuses on the three experiences that define a first visit. It also flies open-jaw — into Marrakech, out of Fez — so you never backtrack. Our flights guide explains how to book that.

Days 1–2: Marrakech

Land in Marrakech and check into a riad in the medina. Because a week is tight, arrange an airport pickup so day one starts smoothly rather than with a luggage-dragging hunt through the lanes.

Day one, ease in — wander the souks, drink mint tea, and let the city's energy wash over you before finding your feet. Day two, hit the highlights: the Bahia Palace, Majorelle Garden, the Koutoubia minaret, and the maze of souks, then Jemaa el-Fnaa at dusk when the square comes alive with food stalls and performers. Two nights is enough for a first taste; our Marrakech guide helps you prioritize.

Days 3–4: Sahara desert tour

Days 3 and 4 are the heart of the week: the standard 3-day/2-night Merzouga tour from Marrakech, which crosses the High Atlas, stops at Aït Benhaddou, and reaches the dunes of Erg Chebbi on the second afternoon. Booking it as a guided tour is what makes a 7-day plan work, because the driving is long and the stops are spread out.

Day 3: over the Atlas

Cross the High Atlas via the Tizi n'Tichka pass, stop at the film-famous kasbah of Aït Benhaddou, and overnight in the Dades or Todra area.

Day 4: the dunes

Through the dramatic Todra Gorge and on to Merzouga, where you'll ride a camel into the dunes of Erg Chebbi to a desert camp — dinner, stargazing, and sunrise over the sand. It's the memory most people rank first. See our Sahara guide.

Days 5–6: Fez

Most desert tours can drop you in Fez rather than returning to Marrakech, which is exactly what you want for an open-jaw trip. Spend two nights exploring Fès el-Bali, the world's largest car-free medieval city. Hire a local guide for your first morning — the medina is a genuine labyrinth — and see the tanneries, the madrasas, and the ancient university. Fez is quieter and more traditional than Marrakech, a fitting final act. Stay in a medina riad.

Day 7: Home

Fly out of Fez (FEZ), or transfer to Casablanca if your flights require it. Because you started in Marrakech and ended in Fez, your week traces a clean line across the country instead of doubling back.

Could you add anything?

If you can stretch to eight or nine days, the natural additions are Chefchaouen (the blue city, a few hours north of Fez) or a day trip to Essaouira from Marrakech for a coastal change of pace. But at exactly seven days, resist the urge — the trip above is already full, and adding more just means more time in transit. If you have more time, step up to our 10-day itinerary, which adds the Atlas and Chefchaouen at a relaxed pace.

What a fast week actually feels like

Be honest with yourself about pace. Seven days moves quickly, and two of them are largely travel days on the desert tour, so the trip has real momentum. That's fine — the momentum is part of what makes it feel like an adventure — but it means you should build the two Marrakech days and two Fez days to be relatively relaxed, letting the medinas soak in rather than racing a checklist. The desert days do the heavy lifting on "wow," and the city days are your breathing room. If you're someone who hates feeling rushed on vacation, either accept that a week is a highlights reel or add a day or two.

An alternative: skip the desert

Not everyone wants two travel-heavy days out of seven. If the long desert drive doesn't appeal, there's a slower alternative: base longer in Marrakech and Fez, add day trips (the Atlas from Marrakech, Meknes and the Roman ruins of Volubilis from Fez), and trade the Sahara for the mountains, which are much closer. You'd miss the dunes — the trip's signature for many — but you'd gain a calmer, less transit-heavy week. There's no wrong choice; it depends on whether the Sahara night is a must-do for you or a nice-to-have. For most first-timers it's the former, which is why the main route centers on it.

Practical notes for the week

Pack light but bring layers for the desert's hot days and cold nights, plus a scarf and comfortable shoes for the medinas. Carry cash — much of this route is cash-only outside hotels. Confirm whether your desert tour ends in Fez or returns to Marrakech before you book flights, so your open-jaw ticket matches. And get an eSIM so you land connected, since a tight week has no room for an arrival-day scramble. The money picture for a short trip is in our cost guide.

Don't skip the food

On a fast week it's tempting to treat meals as fuel, but Moroccan food is half the experience and worth building in a little time for. In Marrakech, eat at least one dinner at a rooftop riad restaurant and brave the food stalls of Jemaa el-Fnaa for the atmosphere. The desert camp dinner — usually a communal tagine under the stars — is a highlight in itself. And Fez, the culinary heart of the country, is the place to try pastilla, the sweet-savory pie the city is famous for. You don't need reservations at fancy places; some of the best meals are the cheapest. A week goes fast, so let a couple of long, unhurried meals be part of the plan rather than an afterthought — see our guide to Moroccan dishes.

Tips for a 7-day trip

Book the desert tour and your riads before you arrive, since a week leaves no slack for figuring it out on the fly. Consider guided vs. independent carefully — a short trip is exactly where a guided desert leg earns its keep. Pack layers for hot desert days and cold nights. And accept that a week is a taster, not the whole meal; most first-timers leave already planning to come back for the parts they missed. What a week forces you to drop, and why, is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

7-day Morocco itinerary FAQ

Is a week enough time for Morocco?

It's enough for the essential first-timer experience — Marrakech, a Sahara night, and Fez — but you'll skip the coast and Chefchaouen. It's a taster, not a complete tour.

Can you visit the Sahara in 7 days?

Yes. A standard 3-day/2-night desert tour from Marrakech fits comfortably into a week and can end in Fez instead of returning.

Should I fly in and out of the same city?

No — fly open-jaw, into Marrakech and out of Fez, so you don't waste a day backtracking across the country.

Is 7 days in Morocco worth it?

Absolutely, if you focus. Trying to see everything in a week backfires; doing three things well makes for a great short trip.

The most popular way to reach the Sahara from Marrakech is an organized multi-day tour, and for good reason: it handles the long drive, the logistics, and the desert camp, turning a daunting journey into a smooth, spectacular trip. Here's exactly what to expect and how to choose a good one.

The standard route: 3 days to Merzouga

The classic tour is a 3-day/2-night loop from Marrakech to the Erg Chebbi dunes near Merzouga and back (or ending in Fez, which many travelers prefer). It's a lot of driving, but the route itself is full of highlights:

Day 1

Cross the High Atlas via the dramatic Tizi n'Tichka pass, stop at the UNESCO kasbah of Aït Benhaddou (a favorite film location), pass through Ouarzazate, and overnight in the Dades or Todra area.

Day 2

Explore the Todra Gorge, then drive on to Merzouga, arriving in time to ride camels into the dunes for sunset, dinner, and a night at a desert camp under the stars.

Day 3

Wake for sunrise over the dunes, then the long drive back to Marrakech — or onward to Fez if you booked the one-way version, which saves backtracking.

A shorter 2-day/1-night option runs to Zagora's smaller dunes if you're tight on time, but most first-timers find the extra day to Merzouga worth it. See our Sahara guide and Merzouga vs. Zagora comparison.

What's included

Most tours cover transport in a 4x4 or minivan, a driver (sometimes a separate guide), accommodation en route, the camel trek into the dunes, dinner and breakfast at the camp, and the desert camp itself. What's usually not included: lunches, drinks, tips for your driver and camp staff, and any upgrades to a luxury camp. Always confirm exactly what's covered before booking, since the cheapest tours often trim inclusions.

Group vs. private tours

Desert tours from Marrakech come in two formats: a shared vehicle with a handful of other travelers, or a private car with your own driver. The route and the camp are usually identical; what changes is the price, the pace, and who decides when you stop. Group tours suit solo travelers and couples watching the budget, private tours suit families and anyone who wants control.

Group tours

Shared vehicle with a handful of other travelers, cheaper, and sociable — many people enjoy the camaraderie of the shared journey. The pace is set by the group and the itinerary is fixed.

Private tours

Your own vehicle and driver, more expensive but flexible — you can stop when you like, adjust the pace, and choose your camp. Good for families, couples, or anyone who values comfort and control. Both deliver the same core experience; it comes down to budget and preference. Our guided vs. independent guide helps you weigh it.

Choosing a camp comfort level

Desert camps range from basic (simple tents, shared facilities) to luxury (private tents with real beds and en-suite bathrooms). Mid-range and luxury camps are surprisingly comfortable and only modestly more expensive — worth it for many first-timers, since it's likely your one desert night. Check what camp tier your tour uses.

What a desert tour costs

Prices vary widely by format and comfort level, so we don't quote a fixed figure — but the pattern is clear. Budget group tours with basic camps are very affordable and popular with younger travelers; mid-range group tours with better camps cost more but remain reasonable; and private tours with luxury camps sit at the top. What drives the price is mostly the camp tier, whether it's group or private, and the number of nights. Be wary of the very cheapest tours, which sometimes cut corners on the camp, cram in too many people, or rush the driving. Reading recent reviews and confirming exactly what's included is the best way to judge value. Our cost guide puts desert tours in the context of a whole trip's budget.

Surviving the long drive

The one honest downside of a Merzouga tour is the driving — it's a lot of hours in a vehicle, especially on the return leg. A few things make it easier: choose the one-way-to-Fez option if it fits your itinerary, so you don't repeat the drive; sit up front if you're prone to car sickness on the mountain switchbacks; bring downloaded music, podcasts, or a book since signal is patchy; and embrace the stops, which are genuinely spectacular rather than filler. The scenery — Atlas passes, kasbahs, gorges, palm oases — is a real part of the experience, not just transit. Frame it that way and the drive becomes a highlight instead of a chore.

Before and after the tour

Because tours start early and end late, plan a night in Marrakech on either side rather than trying to connect straight from a flight. Arrive a day before to rest, sort out cash, and pack a small overnight bag for the camp (you can leave your main luggage at your Marrakech riad, which most will hold for you). On return, you'll be dusty and tired, so a comfortable riad and a relaxed evening are the perfect reset. If your tour ends in Fez instead, book your onward accommodation there and have the same small-bag strategy. A little planning around the tour's edges makes the whole experience smoother.

Tips for booking

A few things that make for a better trip: book ahead in peak spring and fall seasons, when good tours fill up. Read recent reviews closely — driver quality and camp standards vary. Consider the one-way-to-Fez option to avoid a repeat of the long drive. Confirm inclusions and camp tier in writing. And build the tour into your wider plan using our 10-day itinerary, which slots the 3-day desert loop neatly into the classic route.

Choosing group or private is the easy half. The harder half is that the tour you book also fixes which city you end in, how many nights the desert takes out of your week, and what you can still fit afterwards. the complete Morocco trip guide maps how that choice ripples through the rest of the trip.

Sahara tours FAQ

How long is a Sahara tour from Marrakech?

The standard Merzouga trip is 3 days/2 nights; a shorter Zagora option runs 2 days/1 night. The Merzouga route can also end in Fez.

What's included in a desert tour?

Typically transport, driver, en-route accommodation, the camel trek, camp dinner and breakfast, and the desert camp. Lunches, drinks, and tips usually aren't — confirm before booking.

Should I book a group or private tour?

Group tours are cheaper and sociable; private tours cost more but offer flexibility and comfort. Both give the same core desert experience.

Can a Sahara tour end in Fez instead of returning to Marrakech?

Yes — many Merzouga tours offer a one-way option ending in Fez, which fits perfectly into a classic loop and avoids repeating the long drive.

Ask anyone who's been to Morocco where you should stay, and the answer comes back fast: a riad. For a first-timer it's one of the easiest ways to make a trip feel special — but "riad" is a word most Americans arrive not quite understanding. Here's what a riad actually is, why it's worth it, and how to pick one that fits your trip.

What is a riad?

A riad is a traditional Moroccan house or palace built inward around a central courtyard or garden, often with a fountain at its heart and rooms opening onto the open-air middle. The design turns its back on the busy street outside — thick walls, few exterior windows — and opens up internally into a calm, tiled, plant-filled sanctuary. Many have been lovingly restored and converted into small guesthouses, typically with just a handful of rooms, a rooftop terrace, and a level of personal attention closer to a bed-and-breakfast than a hotel.

The magic is the contrast: you step off a chaotic medina lane through an unremarkable door and into a hushed courtyard with a trickling fountain, intricate zellij tilework, and carved cedar. It's a genuinely Moroccan experience you can't really get anywhere else.

Why stay in a riad?

Location inside the medina

Most riads sit inside the old medina, which puts you steps from the souks, squares, and sights — exactly where you want to be, and where cars can't go anyway.

Atmosphere and hospitality

Small size means personal service: staff who help you plan days, arrange a trusted taxi, or serve mint tea when you arrive. Breakfast on a sunny rooftop terrace overlooking the medina is a standard riad pleasure.

A calm base in an intense city

Marrakech and Fez can be gloriously overwhelming. Retreating to the quiet of a riad courtyard at the end of the day is what makes the intensity sustainable.

What to know before you book

Riads are converted courtyard houses inside the medina, and booking one comes with three practical realities: they are genuinely hard to find on arrival, rooms in historic buildings vary enormously in size and light, and stairs are usually unavoidable. Good riads meet you at the nearest car-accessible point and walk you in — message the property before you arrive.

Because they're tucked into the medina maze, riads can be genuinely hard to find on arrival — good ones will arrange to meet you at a car-accessible point and walk you in, so message ahead. Rooms in historic buildings vary; some are small or dark by design, so read recent reviews and look at actual room photos. Not every riad has an elevator or easy luggage access, which matters if stairs are a concern. And while many riads take cards, some smaller ones prefer cash — check when you book.

What's usually included

Most riads include breakfast — often a generous spread of Moroccan breads, pancakes (msemen and beghrir), olives, fresh juice, and mint tea, served on the terrace or in the courtyard. Beyond that, the standout riad extra is service you won't find at a big hotel: staff will book a reliable airport transfer, arrange a trusted local guide, call ahead to a hammam, or even cook a traditional dinner on request with a little notice. Many riads also offer this home-cooked dinner as an option, which is a lovely, low-key first night when you don't want to head back out into the medina. Ask what's on offer when you book — the personal touches are the whole point.

How much do riads cost?

Riads span the full range. A simple, well-run guesthouse in the medina can be genuinely affordable, mid-range riads offer beautiful rooms and rooftop terraces for a comfortable nightly rate, and restored-palace riads climb into luxury territory with plunge pools and spa services. Because the best-reviewed small riads have only a few rooms, they book up — reserve early for peak spring and fall dates. For dollar figures across accommodation tiers, see our Morocco trip cost guide.

Riad or hotel?

You don't have to choose one for the whole trip. A common first-timer approach is to stay in riads in the atmospheric cities — Marrakech, Fez, Chefchaouen — where the experience shines, and opt for a modern hotel where it makes more sense, such as near the airport on a travel day, or in Casablanca. Out in the desert, the equivalent experience is a night in a Sahara desert camp, and in the mountains it's a kasbah or guesthouse. Matching your lodging to each place is part of the fun.

How to book a riad

Riads across Marrakech, Fez, and beyond are listed on the major booking platforms, which makes it easy to compare courtyards, rooftop terraces, locations, and recent guest reviews in one place. Filter by medina location and read the latest reviews closely — for riads more than most stays, the recent guest experience tells you what you're really getting. Once you've found one you love, message the property before arrival to arrange the medina meet-up, and you'll start your trip the right way: stepping out of the noise and into your own tiled courtyard.

Choosing where in the medina

Not all medina locations are equal, and it's worth a moment's thought. A riad deep in the heart of the old city is the most atmospheric but the hardest to reach with luggage; one nearer a main gate (a "bab") or a car-accessible edge is easier to get in and out of, especially on arrival and departure days. Light sleepers should check whether a riad sits near a mosque — the pre-dawn call to prayer carries — or above a busy lane. None of this should scare you off a medina stay; it just helps to read reviews with an eye for the practical, not only the pretty. The best riads strike a balance: immersive enough to feel special, reachable enough that day one doesn't start with a suitcase-dragging odyssey.

For where to base yourself specifically, see our guides to where to stay in Marrakech and the best riads in Marrakech for first-timers.

Where you sleep quietly decides more than comfort: it sets how far you walk, how often you take a taxi, and how much of the medina you meet on foot each day. the complete Morocco trip guide works through the base decision alongside the transport and sequencing calls it drives.

Riad FAQ

What exactly is a riad?

A traditional Moroccan house built around an interior courtyard or garden, often restored into a small, characterful guesthouse with a rooftop terrace.

Are riads worth it for first-timers?

Very much so. They put you inside the medina near the sights, offer personal service, and provide a calm retreat from busy cities — a highlight of most first trips.

Are riads expensive?

They span budgets, from simple guesthouses to lavish restored palaces, so you can find a riad experience at most price points. Book early for the best-reviewed ones.

Is it hard to find a riad in the medina?

It can be — the medina is a maze. Good riads arrange to meet you at a car-accessible point and walk you in, so message the property before you arrive.

Moroccan cuisine is one of the great pleasures of a trip here — fragrant, generous, and built on centuries of Berber, Arab, and Mediterranean influence. For a first-timer, knowing what to order turns every meal into an adventure. Here are the essential dishes and drinks to seek out.

The essential main dishes

Tagine

The dish you'll eat most — a slow-cooked stew named for the conical clay pot it's made in. Classic versions include chicken with preserved lemon and olives, lamb with prunes and almonds, and kefta (meatball) with egg. Endlessly varied and always comforting.

Couscous

Traditionally the Friday family meal — fluffy steamed semolina topped with vegetables and meat. If you see couscous offered on a Friday, that's the day to order it.

Pastilla (bastilla)

A showstopper, especially in Fez — a sweet-and-savory pie of poultry (traditionally pigeon), almonds, and spices in flaky pastry, dusted with cinnamon and sugar. Unexpected and delicious.

Harira

A hearty tomato, lentil, and chickpea soup, especially popular for breaking the fast during Ramadan but served year-round. Comforting and cheap.

Mechoui

Slow-roasted whole lamb, tender and simple, often found at special stalls and celebrations.

Street food and snacks

Some of the best eating is on the street. Look for msemen (flaky square griddle pancakes) and beghrir (spongy "thousand-hole" pancakes) at breakfast; sfenj (North African doughnuts); grilled skewers (brochettes); bowls of snails in spiced broth at the markets; and freshly squeezed orange juice from the stalls in Jemaa el-Fnaa. In coastal Essaouira, don't miss the port's grilled fish. A street food guide helps you choose safely — busy stalls with high turnover are the ones to trust.

What to drink

Mint tea

The national drink and a symbol of hospitality — green tea brewed strong with fresh mint and plenty of sugar, poured theatrically from height. You'll be offered it constantly; accepting is part of the culture.

Coffee and juices

Coffee is popular (often as nous-nous, half coffee half milk), and fresh fruit juices are everywhere and cheap. On the question of alcohol — it's available for tourists in licensed hotels, restaurants, and bars, though not consumed openly in public; our alcohol guide explains.

Breakfast, the underrated meal

Moroccan breakfast deserves its own mention because it's a delight and often included at riads. Expect a spread rather than a single plate: an assortment of breads (including msemen and beghrir pancakes) served with honey, olive oil, amlou (an addictive almond-argan-honey spread), jam, and soft cheese, alongside olives, eggs, fresh orange juice, and of course mint tea or coffee. It's a leisurely, generous start to the day and one of the quiet pleasures of staying in a riad. If your accommodation offers it, lingering over a rooftop breakfast in the morning light is a lovely way to begin before the medina wakes up fully.

The Moroccan meal and hospitality

Eating in Morocco is as much about the ritual as the food. Meals often begin with an array of small salads and warm bread, build to a shared central dish everyone eats from — traditionally with the right hand and a piece of bread as your utensil — and end with fruit, sweets, and tea. Hospitality is central: if you're invited into a home, expect to be fed generously and repeatedly, and refusing outright can cause offense, so pace yourself and accept graciously. Bread (khobz) is sacred and appears at every meal, used to scoop and mop. Understanding this rhythm helps you relax into meals rather than rush them, which is exactly how they're meant to be enjoyed.

Sweets and pastries

Save room for Moroccan sweets: chebakia (sesame, honey-soaked flower-shaped cookies), briouat (sweet stuffed pastries), gazelle horns (kaab el ghazal, almond-filled crescents), and endless date and nut confections, all lovely with mint tea. They're a fixture of hospitality and celebration.

Tips for eating well

A few pointers: eat where locals eat for the best and cheapest food; use your right hand for eating, especially from shared dishes; and consider a cooking class or food tour early in your trip to learn the dishes and shop the souk with a guide — one of the most rewarding activities in the country. Stick to bottled water, and give your stomach a day to adjust before going all-in on street food. Above all, come hungry and curious — Moroccan food is a highlight in its own right.

A note on food safety

Most visitors eat wonderfully in Morocco without any trouble, but a little care prevents the common traveler's stomach. Drink bottled or filtered water and avoid ice from uncertain sources, especially early in your trip. Choose busy stalls and restaurants with high turnover, where food is fresh and constantly cooking. Fruit you can peel yourself is a safe bet. Give your system a day or two to adjust before diving into the most adventurous street food. And carry a basic stomach remedy just in case. None of this should stop you from eating widely — the food is a highlight — it just tilts the odds firmly in your favor so you can enjoy every tagine and pastry. When in doubt, follow the crowds — a stall packed with locals is both a sign of great food and of high, safe turnover. It's the single most reliable rule of thumb for eating well and safely anywhere in Morocco, from a Marrakech square to a roadside stop on the way to the desert.

Moroccan food FAQ

What is the most famous Moroccan dish?

Tagine — a slow-cooked stew named for its conical clay pot — is the most iconic, followed closely by couscous and, in Fez, pastilla.

Is Moroccan food spicy?

Not usually hot-spicy — it's aromatic and warmly spiced (cumin, cinnamon, saffron, ginger) rather than fiery. The condiment harissa adds heat if you want it.

What should vegetarians eat in Morocco?

Vegetable tagines, couscous, lentil and chickpea dishes, salads, and bread are widely available, though always confirm dishes are meat-free, as some use meat broth.

Is street food safe in Morocco?

Generally yes at busy stalls with high turnover. Stick to bottled water, give your stomach a day to adjust, and choose popular spots over quiet ones.

Getting around Morocco is easier than its reputation suggests. Between comfortable trains, reliable long-distance buses, and cheap local taxis, most first-timers can navigate the country without ever renting a car. Here's how each option works and when to use it.

Trains (ONCF): the backbone

Morocco's national rail network, ONCF, is comfortable, punctual, and cost-effective — the best way to travel between the major cities it serves: Casablanca, Rabat, Fez, Marrakech, and Tangier. The Al Boraq high-speed line connects Tangier and Casablanca in a fraction of the old time. Book first class for a reserved seat and a little more comfort, especially on busy routes; second class is cheaper and fine but can be crowded. The key limitation to remember: there is no train to Chefchaouen, Essaouira, or the Sahara — those need buses or other transport. You can check schedules and book on the ONCF website or at station counters.

Buses (CTM and Supratours): filling the gaps

For destinations off the rail network, intercity coaches are the answer, and two companies stand out for reliability and comfort: CTM and Supratours. These are the buses to take to reach Chefchaouen, Essaouira, and the Sahara gateway towns. They're comfortable, air-conditioned, and run on schedules — a world apart from the cheaper local buses. Book ahead in high season, as popular routes sell out. Avoid the informal, unmarked local buses for long trips; the extra few dollars for CTM or Supratours is well worth it.

Taxis: petit and grand

Morocco has two kinds of taxi and they do different jobs. Petit taxis are small metered cars that work only inside a city and take up to three passengers. Grand taxis are older shared sedans running fixed intercity routes, leaving when six passengers have paid. Knowing which one you need before you walk up to the rank saves both confusion and money.

Petit taxis

Small, metered taxis for getting around within a city. They're cheap, but drivers sometimes claim the meter is "broken" — insist on the meter or firmly agree a fare before getting in. They can't leave city limits and typically take up to three passengers.

Grand taxis

Older, larger shared taxis (often Mercedes sedans) that run fixed intercity routes, leaving when full — usually six passengers crammed in. They're a cheap, local way to cover routes without buses, and you can also pay to charter the whole car for a private trip. Agree the price and whether you're sharing or chartering before you set off.

Ride-hailing apps

In larger cities, ride-hail apps like Careem, Heetch, and inDrive operate and can be convenient — you get a set price and skip the meter negotiation. Coverage is best in Casablanca and other big cities; smaller towns rely on traditional taxis. Having a data connection makes these apps usable from the moment you land.

Should you rent a car or hire a driver?

Renting a car gives freedom for rural routes and the mountains, but city driving is chaotic and parking is a headache, so many first-timers skip it — see our car rental guide. A popular middle path is hiring a private driver for specific legs (like the desert or a mountain day), which removes the stress while keeping flexibility. For the long desert journey especially, a driver or organized tour is the norm. Remember Morocco drives on the right, like the U.S., and police checkpoints are common — keep your documents handy.

Domestic flights: usually unnecessary

Morocco does have domestic flights, mostly on Royal Air Maroc and a low-cost affiliate, linking cities like Casablanca, Marrakech, Fez, and the far south. For the compact classic first-timer loop, they're rarely worth it — the cities are close enough that trains and buses are simpler, cheaper, and skip the airport hassle. Flying only really makes sense if you're heading somewhere far-flung like the deep south (Dakhla) or trying to save a long day of overland travel on a tight schedule. For the standard Marrakech–desert–Fez–Chefchaouen route, keep it on the ground; you'll see more and spend less.

Practical tips for smooth travel

A few habits make Moroccan transport easier. Book trains and CTM/Supratours buses in advance during peak spring and fall seasons, when seats sell out. Carry small bills and coins — drivers and stations rarely break large notes easily. Keep some cash on you always, since not everything takes cards. Build buffer time around connections; while trains are punctual, buses and shared taxis run on looser schedules. Have your accommodation's location and a nearby landmark saved offline, because the final approach — especially into a medina — is often on foot. And keep your passport handy on the road for the police checkpoints that are routine on intercity routes, particularly heading south toward the desert.

Putting it together

A typical first-timer combines them all: trains between Marrakech, Casablanca, and Fez; a CTM or Supratours bus to Chefchaouen or Essaouira; petit taxis within cities; and a guided tour or private driver for the Sahara. It's an affordable, flexible mix that covers the whole classic loop without the stress of self-driving. Plan the route with our 10-day itinerary.

Accessibility and comfort notes

A realistic note for those with mobility concerns: Morocco's older medinas, trains, and buses aren't always step-free, and grand taxis can be a tight squeeze. If accessibility matters, a private driver with a comfortable vehicle is the smoothest option and worth the cost, letting you skip crowded stations and cram-full shared taxis. For everyone else, first class on trains and the premium CTM/Supratours buses offer plenty of comfort at low cost. Families with young kids often find a private driver for longer legs removes a lot of stress, while trains are easy and fun for children on the city-to-city hops. Match the transport to your group, and the whole trip flows better.

Each mode here has its own price logic, and they interact: the leg you take by train changes which city you can base in, and the leg you take by grand taxi changes what you should be carrying in cash that morning. the complete Morocco trip guide charts those connections across a full first-timer route.

Getting around Morocco FAQ

Is it easy to get around Morocco without a car?

Yes. Trains link the major cities, CTM and Supratours buses cover the rest, and taxis handle local trips. Most first-timers never need to drive.

Are trains or buses better in Morocco?

Trains are best between the cities they serve (Casablanca, Rabat, Fez, Marrakech, Tangier). For Chefchaouen, Essaouira, and the Sahara — which have no train — take CTM or Supratours buses.

What's the difference between petit and grand taxis?

Petit taxis are metered and stay within a city; grand taxis are shared (or chartered) sedans running fixed intercity routes. Agree fares in advance for both.

Do I need to rent a car in Morocco?
